source: Hastie and Pennington (c.1993) Implications of the Story Model for the Trial Judge's Behavior
finding: The authors state the model in three stages: build a causal story, learn the verdict categories from the judge's instructions, then match story to category. Story quality is coherence = completeness + consistency + plausibility. If two stories are both coherent, uniqueness fails and confidence drops.
numbers: No new numbers. Story coverage of credible-witness evidence is listed as the first factor of confidence.
quote: Confidence in the final decision will be partly determined by the goodness-of-fit of the evidence-solution pairing
limits: A summary written for judges, not the experiments. Only criminal trials; no extreme, racial or emotional cases. Authors say a few jurors did not follow the strategy.
agent_relevance: Gives the exact scoring parts (coverage, coherence parts, uniqueness) that can be coded for hypothesis selection in S7.

source: Hastie and Pennington (c.1993) Implications of the Story Model (judges section)
finding: In a small pilot, judges built stories too, but reasoned backwards from known verdict elements early. They spent more time on credibility and inference chains. In routine cases they skipped element checking and matched the case story to remembered past cases (analogy).
numbers: 4 trial judges, 2 of the stimulus trials (pilot, not systematic).
limits: Pilot only; authors admit no large systematic study of judges.
agent_relevance: Expert pattern: when the category set is known, build the story toward the decisive elements and match to a case library. Supports an analogy step after story building.

source: Hastie and Pennington (c.1993) Implications of the Story Model (juror weaknesses)
finding: Jurors are swayed by story consistency and plausibility and under-weight source credibility and inference-chain strength. Unfamiliar legal terms are reinterpreted through the story (example: 'exhaust all means to avoid combat' read as 'should not have been there'). Non-stereotypic crimes get fewer convictions.
numbers: No numbers given.
limits: Qualitative claim in a review note.
agent_relevance: A fluent coherent story can hide weak evidence links. The agent needs a separate check on each link, not only on story fit (matches G2, G3).

source: Burd, Hans, Phalen et al. (2025) Diverging Decisions? A Comparison of Jury Verdict Procedures (section 1.3.1 reviews Pennington and Hastie 1992)
finding: Secondary account of Pennington and Hastie 1992: mock jurors decided more in line with the evidence when it was shown in chronological story order than when grouped by legal issue. Item-by-item presentation lowered confidence. The authors argue special verdict forms (item by item) may cut decision quality.
numbers: Own studies: Exp 1 N=267 (civil defamation vignette), Exp 2 N=292 (mock trial plus deliberation). General verdict gave more plaintiff wins than special verdict in both.
limits: Secondary summary; the 1992 effect sizes were not quoted. I could not open the 1992 paper itself.
agent_relevance: Supports giving the agent the whole evidence as one ordered narrative before scoring, and warns that forcing separate per-element questions can lower holistic accuracy.

source: Curley, Murray, MacLean et al. (2022) Verdict spotting: juror bias, evidence anchors and verdict system
finding: A test read against the story model: pre-trial bias predicted verdict and belief of guilt, while 'evidence anchors' did not. Authors say two of the three narrative ingredients come from pre-trial knowledge and call the model dominant for about 30 years.
numbers: N=128 mock jurors, two homicide vignettes, within-subject. Two-verdict vs three-verdict (Scottish 'not proven') system shifted verdict frequencies.
limits: Vignettes not trials; within-subject design (jurors saw two trials). Authors claim only 'some support' for the model.
agent_relevance: Prior beliefs fill story gaps. An agent should flag its prior as an input, since it shapes the story it builds.

source: Lilley, Mojtahedi, Willmott (2026) Intimate partner rape: do rape myths still influence verdict outcomes
finding: Mock jurors with higher rape-myth acceptance gave more not-guilty verdicts; legal attitudes did not predict verdict. Authors read this as story model support: missing facts are filled with prior schemas. The high conviction rate is explained as a narrative with high coherence and coverage that beat the stereotype.
numbers: Sample size not extracted by me.
limits: Post-hoc fit to the model: it can explain either outcome (a falsifiability worry).
agent_relevance: The gap-filling step is where bias enters. Mark every inferred (not observed) story link and keep it out of the coverage count.

source: Sun, Zappala, Di Maso, Pompedda, Nyman, Santtila (2025) Large language models (LLMs) as jurors, Law and Human Behavior
finding: GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet and o1 replicated a human mock-jury study (Fraser 2023). LLMs gave higher mean guilt probability but far fewer guilty verdicts. They showed the same bias against White defendants and the same rise with more allegations, but unlike humans were sensitive to reporting delay (shorter delay, more guilt).
numbers: 2x2x2x3 design, 2,304 responses. Mean guilt probability 63.56 (LLM) vs 58.82 (human). Guilty verdicts 21% (LLM) vs 49% (human).
limits: Abstract only read (full text paywalled). Vignette judgments, not story construction. No story-model measures in the abstract.
agent_relevance: A model's probability and its verdict threshold are separate. Never copy a human threshold; calibrate the verdict step on its own.

source: Bessis, Wills, Wojciechowski, White, Pothos (2026) Legal Decision Biases in GPT: A Comparison with Human Judgment, Behavioral Sciences 16(3):437
finding: GPT-4o showed a strong recency effect: guilt ratings were higher when incriminating evidence came last. GPT-5.2 showed the same effect but smaller. Both changed final ratings when asked for an intermediate judgment, but GPT-4o's was a general inflation unlike the human pattern.
numbers: 720 trials per model per prompt, six Polish criminal cases, scale 1-10. GPT-4o final guilt: G-I single 3.54, G-I double 4.24, I-G single 4.77, I-G double 6.04; order F(1,711)=424.76. GPT-5.2: G-I single 4.79, double 4.75; I-G single 5.02, double 5.35; order F(1,711)=71.24. Temperature 0.2 vs 1 cell means r=0.996 (4o), 0.989 (5.2).
limits: Human data came from Wojciechowski et al. 2025 (120 participants, 715 final ratings), not rerun. Single-number rating, not stories. English translation of Polish cases.
agent_relevance: Evidence order moves a model's verdict score by 1 to 2 points on a 10 scale. Shuffle or reverse evidence order in code and require the verdict to hold (G3 style); avoid asking for intermediate verdicts.

source: Bessis et al. (2026) Legal Decision Biases in GPT: prompt engineering conditions
finding: Three system-prompt fixes (PE1 act as a legal expert, PE2 be meticulous and take time, PE3 be ready to justify with case details) did little. Only PE2 reliably shrank GPT-4o's order effect, and it never vanished. The intermediate-rating inflation was unchanged by any prompt.
numbers: GPT-4o order x prompt F(3,2859)=3.11, p=0.026. PE2 cut the order effect by 0.32 points (SE 0.11, p=0.003) vs PE0; PE1 -0.19 (p=0.075); PE3 -0.16 (p=0.12). Rating x prompt F(3,2859)=1.23, p=0.30.
limits: Three prompts only, from OpenAI guidance; authors call them illustrative.
agent_relevance: Telling the model to be careful is weak against order bias. Structural fixes (code-controlled order permutation, G4/G5) are the better bet than persona or justify prompts. Supports G1.

source: Ersoz (2026) 12 Angry AI Agents: Multi-Agent LLM Decision-Making Through Cinematic Jury Deliberation
finding: Twelve LLM jurors with film personas debated the 12 Angry Men case. Almost all runs ended hung; the lone dissenter almost never converted the majority. Authors name anchoring on the initial vote as the main failure. GPT-4o ignored an 'open-minded' instruction; Llama-4-Scout used it.
numbers: 18 runs (2 models x 3 conditions x N=3). 17 of 18 hung. GPT-4o mean 1.0 vote changes per run; Llama-4-Scout 2.0 (baseline) to 6.0 (open-minded). Only 1 of 3 Llama no-initial-vote runs reached NOT_GUILTY.
limits: Exploratory, tiny N, personas carry preset votes, one film case.
agent_relevance: Multi-agent juries from one model stagnate on the first position, matching G4 (samples are not independent). A lone correct dissent is not enough.

source: Ersoz (2026) 12 Angry AI Agents: design details
finding: Setup: initial vote 11 guilty, 1 not guilty; vote prompt every 12 turns; max 150 turns; run ends as HUNG_JURY after a long stretch with zero vote changes. The paper links deliberative flexibility to RLHF intensity rather than capability (a hypothesis from two models).
numbers: Max turns 150; vote check every 12 turns; 12 agents.
limits: RLHF claim rests on two models.
agent_relevance: Do not assume 'consider other views' prompts work across models; test per model. Prefer code-set rules over prompt wording.

source: Dalal, Valentino, Freitas, Buitelaar (2025) Inference to the Best Explanation in Large Language Models (IBE-Eval)
finding: A scorer picks the best of competing LLM-written causal explanations using four features: logical consistency, parsimony (proof depth, concept drift), coherence, and linguistic uncertainty. The combination beat a GPT-3.5-as-judge baseline. Consistency alone was weak because LLMs rationalize even bad explanations. Uncertainty wording was the strongest single predictor.
numbers: Up to 77% accuracy picking the right explanation (random 50%), +17.5% on average over the GPT-3.5 judge. One model on COPA: coherence .66 alone, uncertainty .70 alone, all features .77. Datasets COPA (500 test) and E-CARE.
limits: Short two-way causal QA, not trial-length evidence. Features computed with a Prolog solver and entailment model on LLM-generated proofs.
agent_relevance: Closest code-scored version of 'pick the story with best coherence'. Consistency is cheap for an LLM to fake, so do not use it as the only gate; parsimony and hedge counts add signal.

source: Dalal et al. (2025) IBE-Eval: regression of criteria on accuracy
finding: Wrong explanations had deeper proofs, more concept drift and lower coherence. Higher linguistic uncertainty went with lower accuracy for all LLMs tested; GPT-3.5 was most consistent.
numbers: Incorrect explanations had about 6% greater proof depth and 10% greater concept drift on average; about 2% of cases were self-evident (tautological) explanations.
limits: Correlational; options were supplied, not found.
agent_relevance: Gives cheap checks (steps, drift, hedges) usable on any story the agent builds before it commits.

source: Fu, Zheng, Yeong, Lam (2026) VeriScene: Reconstructing Crime Scenes from Legal Evidence via World-Model Agent
finding: An agent fuses photos and witness statements into a cited narrative under a code audit loop (3 rounds), then probes physics in a world model. Per-claim citations make evidence coverage countable. The end-to-end multimodal LLM baseline drops evidence and blends contradictory statements.
numbers: 25 scenarios, 7 case types, 139 photos, 65 statements with planted unreliability; 20 test scenes. Evidence coverage 0.9014 (baseline 0.000, no citations). Factual consistency 0.7217 vs 0.6000 (+20.3%). Temporal coherence 0.2900 vs 0.2150 (+34.9%). Without fusion audit coverage fell 0.9014 to 0.8436. Cost $1.82 per scene. Dropping testimonies cut FC to 0.2983.
limits: Synthetic scenes with planted unreliability; authors' own metrics. Story-building stage only; no verdict stage.
agent_relevance: A working LLM-loop version of 'story with coverage': require each claim to cite an item, compute coverage in code, repeat until the audit passes. Matches code-selects (G5).

source: Fu et al. (2026) VeriScene: weak orchestrator tier
finding: A cheap orchestrator kept evidence coverage high (the code checks do the work) but temporal ordering of events collapsed. Stronger models mainly improved event ordering.
numbers: Haiku tier at $0.13 per scene: coverage 0.936, temporal coherence 0.118, visual fidelity 0.480. Opus TC 0.375 vs Flash 0.220. 14x cheaper than the $1.82 tier.
limits: Single paper, own benchmark.
agent_relevance: Coverage can be enforced by code even with a weak model; the causal order of a story needs the strong model.

source: Sprague, Ye, Bostrom, Chaudhuri, Durrett (2024) MuSR: Testing the Limits of Chain-of-Thought with Multistep Soft Reasoning (ICLR)
finding: Murder-mystery narratives (about 1000 words) require checking each suspect for motive, means and opportunity. GPT-4 reached 80.4% with a CoT prompt that describes the strategy; humans 94.1%.
numbers: Murder mystery: random 50.0; GPT-4 80.4; GPT-3.5 61.6; Llama2-70b 48.8; human 94.1. GPT-4 by prompt: Regular 64.8, CoT 65.6, CoT+ 80.4, 1-shot CoT+ 86.0, few-shot 84.8. GPT-3.5: 59.2, 56.0, 61.6, 70.0, 68.4.
limits: Synthetic, generated with GPT-4; two suspects; closer to element matching than story construction.
agent_relevance: Naming the strategy (check each candidate against motive, means, opportunity) added about 15 points for GPT-4 over plain CoT. This is the 'match story to verdict elements' stage in prompt form.

source: Sprague et al. (2024) MuSR: decomposed prompting on murder mysteries
finding: Hard-coding the breakdown (motive, means, opportunity per suspect, count proving facts in code) did not beat end-to-end GPT-4 with the described strategy zero-shot, but did with one example.
numbers: Decomposed prompting 77.6 vs GPT-4 CoT+ 80.4; Decomposed 1-shot 86.0.
limits: Random tie-breaking; one dataset.
agent_relevance: Code-side element counting is competitive but not clearly better than a well-described prompt; a worked example mattered more.

source: Del and Fishel (2023) True Detective: A Deep Abductive Reasoning Benchmark Undoable for GPT-3 and Challenging for GPT-4
finding: 191 long detective puzzles (about 1200 words) test finding the best explanation. Plain GPT-4 and GPT-3.5 were near chance. Giving GPT-4 the author's reasoning chain (golden CoT) took it to 83%. So reaching the explanation, not the final check, is the hard step.
numbers: Random 24%; human average 47%; top-10 humans 80-90%. Vanilla GPT-4 27%, GPT-4 CoT 38%, GPT-3.5 (PPO) CoT 29%. With golden CoT: GPT-3.5 PPO 63%, GPT-4 83%.
limits: Multiple choice; human solve rate from a public site, first tries only; puzzle leakage into training data not ruled out.
agent_relevance: Story generation is the bottleneck. A coverage scorer cannot help if no good candidate story is generated; spend budget on diverse candidate stories first.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Chinese Court Simulation with LLM-Based Agent System (SimCourt)
finding: Judge, prosecutor, attorney, defendant and stenographer agents with memory, planning and reflection, run over a five-stage procedure, predicted imprisonment, probation and fines better than baselines. Human experts rated its agents above real trial participants on recordings.
numbers: Precise rates not extracted by me.
limits: Chinese criminal law; I read only the abstract, intro and setup.
agent_relevance: Shows a stage order (evidence presentation, then debate, then judgement) used as scaffold.

source: He et al. (2024) AgentsCourt: Judicial Decision-Making Agents with Court Debate Simulation and Legal Knowledge Augmentation
finding: A multi-stage agent (determine facts, plaintiff and defendant debate, judge with retrieved laws and precedents) beat prior methods on judgment generation for Chinese cases.
numbers: F1 gains of 8.6% (first instance) and 9.1% (second instance) over existing advanced frameworks.
limits: Chinese cases; metric is charge and sentence match, not story correctness.
agent_relevance: Adds rule and precedent retrieval to the story-to-category match, the analogy step Hastie reports for judges.

source: Chen et al. (2026) Civil Court Simulation with Large Language Models
finding: Five-stage civil court multi-agent simulation with memory and statute retrieval. Memory quality had a large effect on downstream simulation quality; strengths were liability allocation and multi-item judgments.
numbers: No figure extracted (abstract level).
limits: Abstract only.
agent_relevance: In a long-case loop, the stored case summary (the story) is the main quality lever; poor memory of the story gives poor verdicts.

source: Siedler (2026) Strategic Persuasion with Trait-Conditioned Multi-Agent Systems for Iterative Legal Argumentation
finding: Prosecution and defense teams of LLM agents with rhetorical traits argue before an LLM judge. Mixed-trait teams beat uniform ones; moderate interaction depth gave more stable verdicts. The judge outcome depends on persuasion style as well as evidence.
numbers: 10 synthetic cases, 84 three-trait team configurations, over 7,000 trials, DeepSeek-R1 and Gemini 2.5 Pro.
limits: Synthetic cases; judge is an LLM, so fluent argument is rewarded.
agent_relevance: An LLM judge is moved by rhetoric. Do not let a model pick between two competing stories on persuasiveness; score coverage in code (G5).

source: Nguyen, Pham, Sun (2025) AUTOLAW: Legal Compliance via Case Law Generation and Jury-Inspired Deliberation
finding: Voting by a selected pool of LLM jurors raised violation detection over plain majority vote. Juror selection by synthesized expertise helped; role assignment was inconsistent; demonstrations helped everywhere.
numbers: Case-SG detection: individual jurors at least 80.95 to 88.10 in pools P7-P9; AUTOLAW 100 in four voting settings and 97.62 in the rest, above majority vote.
limits: Detects explicit violations in easy real cases (authors say so); not fact finding from conflicting evidence.
agent_relevance: Weighted voter selection helped, but samples from related models are not independent (G4). Weak support only.

source: Chun, Elkins, Lee (2026) AgenticSimLaw: courtroom multi-agent debate for explainable tabular decision making
finding: Prosecutor, defense and judge debate in 7 structured turns on recidivism prediction, compared with CoT across about 90 model and strategy combinations. The debate gave more stable accuracy and F1 across models but only negligible gains over the best zero-shot run.
numbers: NLSY97 data, label 72% NO / 28% YES. Best classic baseline Random Forest accuracy 0.7606, Extra Trees AUC 0.6559.
limits: Tabular recidivism, not narrative evidence.
agent_relevance: A debate frame bought stability, not accuracy. Use an adversarial story pair only when stability matters.

source: Thagard (2003) Why wasn't O.J. convicted? Emotional coherence in legal inference, Cognition and Emotion 17(3):361-383
finding: The ECHO explanatory-coherence network, run on the O.J. Simpson evidence network, accepted that Simpson was the killer (and that police tried to frame him), so pure coherence maximizing did not reproduce the jury's not-guilty verdict. Treating the guilt hypothesis as inhibited (presumption of innocence) can reject it if the inhibition is large enough. The author prefers emotional coherence as the explanation.
numbers: No juror sample; one case network (Figure 2). Four accounts compared: explanatory coherence, Bayesian network (JavaBayes), wishful thinking, emotional coherence.
limits: Single case study with hand-built network; a different network the jurors held cannot be ruled out. The paper notes jurors also may have found reasonable doubt, not lower coherence.
agent_relevance: Shows the verdict stage is not just 'best story wins': a burden-of-proof margin must be added on top of coverage and coherence. Encode a threshold, not an argmax.

source: Willmott, Boduszek, Debowska, Woodfield (2018) Introduction and validation of the Juror Decision Scale (JDS): an empirical investigation of the story model
finding: A questionnaire built to measure story-model constructs in jurors (cited by Lilley 2026 as support for the model). The landing page returned 403 and I did not read it.
numbers: Not read.
limits: Unopened; title and citations only.
agent_relevance: Possible source of item wording for scoring story constructs.
